content:
It’s not the hours. It’s not the job. It’s the one thing almost everyone loses right before they break.

5 min read
Just now

--

Burnout looks like a workload problem. After enough conversations with exhausted people, I stopped believing that’s the real story.
A nurse, wiped out after a twelve hour shift. A teacher, wiped out after a six hour day that somehow never ends at six hours. A freelancer with an empty calendar, wiped out from a week where nothing technically went wrong. A parent who hasn’t worked a paid job in years, wiped out by 9am. Different lives, different responsibilities, and somehow the same sentence comes out of almost all of them eventually: “I don’t even know what I’m so tired from.” Not the task itself. Something underneath it.
The workload explanation is tidy. It’s also incomplete more often than people admit. Two people can carry the exact same load, same deadlines, same responsibilities, same number of demands on their time, and one comes apart while the other doesn’t. If hours alone caused it, that gap shouldn’t exist. Something else is doing most of the damage, and it shows up in every kind of life, not just the obviously overworked one.
What the research actually says
Psychologist Christina Maslach has spent close to five decades studying burnout, and her Areas of Worklife model, developed with Michael Leiter, names six specific mismatches between a person and their environment that predict it: workload, control, reward, community, fairness, and values. Workload is on that list. It’s just not the only one, and on its own, it’s a surprisingly weak predictor. Control shows up again and again as one of the strongest, and it applies just as much to a stay at home parent or a shift worker as it does to anyone behind a desk.
Research across thousands of people, spanning healthcare, education, retail, caregiving, and office work, has repeatedly shown burnout tracking more closely with conditions than with individual resilience or weakness. Control, in this research, doesn’t mean being in charge. It means something narrower and more universal: having some say over how your day actually unfolds. Whether you can push back a demand that doesn’t make sense. Whether you can say no without a cost you can’t afford. Whether your time, once it’s been handed over, still belongs to anyone at all.
Maslach has made the same point publicly, more than once: when someone starts doing the bare minimum instead of their best, that’s usually not proof they’ve gotten lazier. It’s a sign that something in the structure around them has broken, not something in them. Most burnout advice gets this backwards, treating exhaustion as a stamina problem to be fixed with an app or a weekend off. The research says the opposite. The exhaustion isn’t the malfunction. It’s the appropriate response to something structurally broken.
The same thread, wearing different clothes
Comparison usually isn’t about the other person’s success. It’s about losing control of your own definition of success, because someone else’s yardstick got handed to you, and at some point you stopped noticing you never agreed to use it.
Guilt about rest usually isn’t about laziness. It’s about losing control of your own permission to stop, because somewhere along the way “earning” rest became a requirement, and nobody remembers voting on that rule.
Always being reachable usually isn’t about being helpful. It’s about losing control of your own time, because every notification is a small, repeated reminder that your hours aren’t fully yours, even off the clock, even on a day meant to be your own.
Performed effort, staying visible, answering something late at night just to be seen answering it, usually isn’t about getting more done. It’s about losing control of how your value gets judged. When being seen replaces actual output as the thing that gets rewarded, working past the point of usefulness stops being wasteful and starts being rational.
Different situations, different lives, one mechanism underneath most of them. Something that used to be yours to decide is now being decided somewhere else, and you’ve quietly rebuilt your whole routine around that without ever agreeing to it out loud. Call it the control loss theory of burnout. It’s rarely about how much you’re carrying. It’s almost always about who gets to decide how you carry it.
A phone call during summer vacation
At the start of July, right after summer vacation began, a friend of mine, a teacher, called me. I was mid rant about my own week, something about a deadline I’d let creep up on me, and she went quiet for a second. Then she said she’d been feeling exhausted too. Nine days into vacation. No lesson plans, no alarms, nothing that should explain it.
I laughed and said at least she had the whole summer ahead of her. She didn’t laugh back. She said, “I don’t think it’s about the time off. I think I just forgot how to stop.”
That line stayed with me longer than anything else in the conversation. If rest alone fixed burnout, nine days off should have been more than enough. It wasn’t, and she knew it wasn’t, which is why she called in the first place.
I asked her, once we got past the small talk, what she’d actually change if she could change exactly one thing. Not the hours. Not the pay. One thing.
She didn’t say less work. She said, almost immediately, “I want to be able to tell a parent I’ll answer tomorrow, not tonight, and not feel like I’m about to get in trouble for it.” That’s not a workload complaint. That’s a control complaint wearing a workload costume, and once you know to listen for it, you’ll start hearing it in nearly everyone who describes themselves as burned out, whatever they do for a living.
What this actually means for you
If you’re exhausted right now, the workload question is probably the wrong first question. The more useful one: where, specifically, did you lose the ability to say no, or to stop, or to decide when something is actually finished? That’s usually a smaller, more specific answer than “everything is too much,” and because it’s specific, it’s something you can actually push back on, one boundary at a time, instead of trying to fix an entire life at once.
Maybe the question was never how do I get better at handling pressure. Maybe it’s why did I lose the ability to decide what pressure I was willing to carry in the first place.
